A demo shows query_model being called with an input like 'what do llamas eat' and specifying a model such as Llama 3.
torch.nn.functional.cross_entropy(logits_flat, targets_flat) computes the final loss between output logits and targets from flattened tensors.
The function internally applies softmax to logits to obtain probabilities.
The function selects probabilities corresponding to the target indices/classes.
Cross-entropy loss is computed by taking the negative log of the selected probabilities and averaging (mean) them.
A single line/function call performs all these steps automatically.
Inputs such as token sequences pass through the GPT architecture to produce a logits tensor.
The logits tensor is flattened/merged across batches into logits_flat before loss computation.
In an ideal model, probabilities at target indices should be close to 1 because predictions match targets.
In an unoptimized LLM, target probabilities are initially small, and training aims to increase them toward 1.
In the term 'large language model,' 'large' refers to the large number of parameters in the model.
Before LLMs, model sizes were not very big compared to modern LLMs.
Model size means the number of parameters in the model.
LLMs typically have billions of parameters, and some have trillions of parameters.
Examples of GPT-3 model sizes include 125 million, 350 million, 760 million, 13 billion, and 175 billion parameters.
In GPT model names such as '175B,' the suffix indicates the number of parameters (175 billion).
GPT-4 has even more parameters than GPT-3.
As models progress from GPT-1 to GPT-2 to GPT-3, they become better and their parameter counts increase tremendously.
From GPT-1 to GPT-2 the parameter count increased roughly from 100 million to almost 1 billion (about a 10x increase), and from GPT-2 to GPT-3 there was about a 100x increase.
Original final output layer took 768-dimensional embeddings as input and produced 50,257 outputs corresponding to vocabulary size.
For the classification task, the original output layer was replaced with a classification head.
The classification head takes 768 inputs and produces 2 outputs representing spam or no spam.
Given an input such as 'do you have time', each token produces two outputs corresponding to spam or no spam.
For classification, only the output corresponding to the last token is used.
The last token representation contains information about previous tokens through attention weights.
With batch size 1 and four tokens, the output tensor shape is 1 x 4 x 2.
In the example sequence, the four tokens are 'do', 'you', 'have', and 'time'.
The tokenizer creates a vocabulary of tokens; GPT-2 and the constructed model use a vocabulary size of 50,257.
GPT-2 used a context length of 1024, while the example model uses 256 so it can train locally in a few minutes with lower compute requirements.
The same code can support longer context lengths if enough compute power and memory are available.
The embedding dimension projects token embeddings into a higher-dimensional space to capture semantic meaning.
The number of attention heads refers to the number of self-attention mechanism blocks within one transformer.
There are many transformer blocks, and the layer count specifies how many transformer blocks the model has.
The dropout rate is a configurable dropout-layer parameter and can be set to zero.
The query-key-value bias setting means no bias term is used when initializing the query, key, and value weight matrices.

The GPT model pipeline: input tokens are converted to token embeddings, positional embeddings are added, dropout is applied, the result passes through transformer blocks, then a final normalization layer produces logits.
The returned logits consist of outputs aligned with token positions and vocabulary entries.
Fine-tuning happens after pre-training: a model is first brought to a knowledgeable state, then trained on a specific dataset to further improve weights and parameters.
Loading a pre-trained LLM means using pretrained GPT-2 weights.
A smaller GPT-2 model (~124M/117M parameters) did not perform well for instruction fine-tuning, so a larger model is needed.
The lecture chooses GPT-2 medium with 355 million parameters instead of the smallest model.
The GPT-2 medium model requires approximately 1.42 GB of storage space.
The instructor notes they are running the setup on a 2020 MacBook Air without a fancy GPU.
GPT-2 medium has context size 1024, 24 transformer blocks, and 16 attention heads per block.
The base configuration includes a vocabulary size of 50,257 and context length 1024.
A maximum length parameter is used for encoded texts; by default it is the length of the longest email/text in the dataset, but the user can also externally specify a maximum length.
Texts shorter than the maximum length are padded using pad token ID 50256.
The first preprocessing step is tokenization.
A byte pair encoder (BPE) tokenizer is used.
The tokenizer encodes each sentence/text by converting it into tokens and then mapping those tokens to token IDs using the vocabulary.
The CSV file is read with pandas into a data object.
Every email or text message in the dataset is converted into a sequence of token IDs.
The longest_encoded_length functionality computes the maximum encoded length across all text messages in the dataset.
D_out equals head dimension multiplied by number of heads.
The last dimension of the keys, queries, and values tensors is reshaped/unrolled into separate number-of-heads and head-dimension dimensions.
Example: with D_out = 6 and number of heads = 2, the head dimension is 3.
Example reshape: tensors of shape 1 × 3 × 6 become 1 × 3 × 2 × 3 after splitting into heads and head dimensions.

Interpretation of a 1 × 3 × 2 × 3 tensor: ignore the batch dimension; the size 3 corresponds to tokens/rows, the size 2 corresponds to attention heads within each token, and the final size 3 corresponds to the vector dimension within each head.
Categorical cross-entropy is computed by taking the probabilities at the target indices, applying log/negative log likelihood, and averaging them.
The training goal is to reduce categorical cross-entropy loss as close to zero as possible.
Perplexity is a modified form of cross-entropy loss.
Perplexity measures how well the model's predicted probability distribution matches the actual distribution of words in the dataset.
Perplexity is a more interpretable way to understand model uncertainty when predicting the next token.
Lower perplexity means better predictions.
Perplexity is calculated as the exponent of the loss.
A perplexity of 48725 means the model is as uncertain as randomly choosing the next token from about 48725 vocabulary tokens.
The vocabulary size mentioned is about 50,257 tokens.
For the input 'every effort moves', a perplexity of 48725 means the model effectively must choose among 48725 possible next tokens, indicating high uncertainty and poor performance.
A perplexity score of 2 would indicate much lower uncertainty and good prediction quality.
